short: Diocletian roughly doubled the number of provinces and grouped them into twelve dioceses, reshaping how the empire was governed.
full:
Beginning in the mid-290s, Diocletian broke up the empire's roughly fifty existing provinces into around one hundred smaller units, each easier for a governor to control and harder for an ambitious one to use as a base for revolt. The new provinces were grouped into twelve dioceses, each overseen by a vicarius answering to a praetorian prefect, adding a fresh layer of administration between the provinces and the imperial court.

The reform also separated civil governors from military command wherever possible, a division sharpened further under Constantine. Dioceses and their vicars remained the basic framework of late Roman government for the rest of the western empire's existence and far longer in the east, outlasting the fifth-century collapse of imperial authority in Gaul, Spain and Italy even as the emperors who administered through it did not.
